catalog_quote: [Wilson 1986:287] All of the Wakashan languages distinguish between light and heavy syllables, that is, between non-branching and branching rimes. In Kwakiutlan, a light syllable contains a reduced vowel. A heavy syllable contains a full vowel (which may appear on the surface as either long or short), or a reduced vowel followed by a tautosyllabic sonorant that fills the second V-slot in the branching rime. The basic stress rule of Kwakwala places primary stress on the first heavy syllable in a word. Secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables after the primary stress. Epenthetic schwas, which are inserted after stress assignment, are therefore not counted in placing secondary stresses. ... sweep_summary: search for kwak1269 (Kwak'wala, catalog classification weight, deciding source Wilson 1986 BLS 12:287-288) had a single title item: Bach 1975, 'Long vowels and stress in Kwakiutl', Texas Linguistic Forum 2:9-19, already in our bibliography. It is unambiguously about word stress in this language (Glottolog record 671236; Bach's own publication list and Northern Wakashan checklist, the Internet Archive copies saved). No open copy could be found: no DOI/record on Crossref, Semantic Scholar or OpenAlex; archive.org has other TLF volumes but not 1975; the the Internet Archive index of both of Bach's UMass sites shows only three unrelated PDFs; Google Books lists the 1975 TLF volume (id rPZhaRgAEusC, 186 pp.) with no view; HathiTrust, Google Books pages and WorldCat are bot-walled by automated download; this compilation's was already exhausted. Access = print only, priority high (it is the classic first-hand rule statement and the source every later description cites). Its rule is, however, quoted verbatim in the held Janzen 2015 thesis (p.44, scanned verified in this search of works with stress in the title): 'Stress first syllable with long vowel or vowel plus tautosyllabic resonant or if none stress last syllable', and Gordon 2000 and Werle 2010 (both held) transmit the same leftmost-heavy-else-final rule from Bach 1975; so as far as it can be read second-hand it confirms the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and does not supersede Wilson 1986. Nothing new was read first-hand, so no new stress statement was found; three bibliographic pages were and logged in there.

new_statements.quote: As noted above, the stress pattern of Kʷak̓ʷala is described in the literature as default-to-right (Wilson 1978, Wilson 1986, Shaw 2009). [...] Guc̓a follows this pattern of lexical stress. [...] Any syllable with a full vowel nucleus, or with a schwa followed by a plain resonant in coda position, will attract stress, and the first such syllable from the left edge of a word will bear primary stress. If there are only light syllables in a word, the rightmost syllable is stressed. Light syllables are those with a schwa nucleus, such as open syllables with schwa, or schwa followed by a coda obstruent (ə, əO).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kwak'wala (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule; this work supplies it: leftmost heavy (full V or əR), else final. Note the citation is wrong: this is a UC Santa Barbara PhD dissertation (committee Genetti, Gordon, Mithun, Shaw; eScholarship item 2j88d8vb; 158 pp.), not a UBC MA thesis. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the leftmost heavy syllable of the word; heavy = full (non-schwa) vowel nucleus, or schwa plus a plain (non-glottalized) resonant coda; if no syllable is heavy, the final syllable is stressed ('default-to-right'). Acoustic correlates: longer duration, higher intensity/F0 on the stressed syllable (sec. 3.4.2).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Guc̓a (no statement on secondary stress in the thesis).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 68: 'a full vowel followed by a glottal stop (Vʔ) does not attract stress and, second, neither does a schwa followed by a glottalized resonant (əR')' — glottalization makes the syllable light; n. 18: word-final schwa is banned (would-be schwas are /a/), so some 'default' cases look like final full vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: Siemens 2016 describes the Guc̓a (Quatsino) dialect of Kwak'wala (Wallas family recordings, 2011-2014) and reports the same pattern as the general Kwak'wala literature (Wilson 1978 on Quatsino; Shaw 2009). Hall 1889 is the Alert Bay missionary grammar of 'Kwagiutl'. The catalog citation for Siemens is wrong: it is a UC Santa Barbara PhD dissertation (eScholarship 2j88d8vb, 158 pp.), not a UBC MA thesis.

new_statements.quote: In sum, Kwak’wala stress system can be restated as follows. Stress falls on the leftmost moraic syllable or the rightmost syllable if there is no moraic syllable in the word. ‘Moraic syllable’ refers to a syllable with a non-schwa nucleus or a plain sonorant coda. In the latter case, the nucleus is usually a non-moraic schwa. (p. 325) [On Zec 1988/1995, p. 323:] According to her analysis, primary stress falls on the leftmost syllable containing a long vowel or the rightmost syllable if there is no syllable containing a long vowel in the word. Despite its popularity, it has been pointed out that Zec’s analysis crucially relies on the controversial assumption that vowel length is contrastive in Kwak’wala (Bach et al. 2005).

new_statements.quote: Kwakw’ala (Boas 1947; Bach 1975; Wilson 1986) is typically described as a language with a default-to-right stress system, in which the leftmost heavy syllable (=CVV, CVR [R=sonorant]) attracts stress, otherwise the final syllable, as in (2). (p. 101) [...] Boas reports that stems with initial CV, CVO have accent on second or a later syllable (Boas, pg. 218). This leaves open the possibility that words with more than two syllables may have stress on the second syllable, which would be non-final. Such a stress pattern, which actually occurs frequently in Boas’ data, contradicts the default-to-opposite pattern. [...] Without this information, it is difficult to speak confidently of Kwakw’ala as a language with default-to-opposite stress. (p. 109)

new_statements.quote: [p. 10, verified against the page image] From these examples it would appear that if we have several syllables meeting our tentative condition (long vowel or VRC with R a resonant) the first takes stress. So we might state a rule as follows: A. Stress first syllable with long vowel or vowel plus tautosyllabic resonant or if none stress last syllable. [p. 11] It should be noted that for BASIC STRESS (and some other rules) the resonants (sonorants) include the plain and voiced laterals and nasals, not the glottalized ones. [...] At this point, we have a rule that treats sequences of short vowels and tautosyllabic resonants in the same way as long vowels. [fn. 4, p. 17] Further work remains to be done especially on the behavior of stress in many types of stem extensions, and on stress reduction in long, morphemically complex items, which sometimes seem to have secondary stresses.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Wilson 1986: primary stress on the first heavy syllable, heavy = full vowel or reduced vowel + tautosyllabic sonorant) - Bach 1975 is in fact the earlier source of that generalization: first syllable with long vowel or V + tautosyllabic plain resonant, else the LAST syllable. It states explicitly the default-to-final clause, the restriction to plain (non-glottalized) resonants, and the morphophonemic alternations that feed/bleed weight; fully consistent with the statements held by the project (Siemens 2016, Noguchi 2011 'leftmost moraic syllable or the rightmost syllable', Gordon 2000 default-to-right citing Bach) and with Littell 2016 (work 1)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Unbounded quantity-sensitive 'default-to-opposite' (first/last) stress: primary stress falls on the first (leftmost) syllable of the word that has a long (full, non-schwa) vowel or a vowel followed by a tautosyllabic plain resonant (m n l and glides; glottalized resonants do not count); if the word has no such syllable, stress falls on the last syllable (Rule A; formalized as Rule D, V -> +stress / #X__ where X contains no long vowel and no VRC). Bach treats most surface long vowels as underlying short vowel + resonant sequences, so 'heavy' reduces to V+R; morphophonemic hardening/softening suffixes that glottalize a resonant or turn an obstruent into a resonant move syllables out of or into the heavy class and shift stress accordingly (exx. 26-28), and plural glottal-stop insertion after a high vowel removes that syllable from the stress domain (ǝ́wsgǝmi sg. vs plural with later stress, exx. 49-50).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not analysed: fn. 4 says stress reduction in long, morphemically complex words 'which sometimes seem to have secondary stresses' remains to be worked out and notes that Boas sometimes writes several stress marks in a long word.
new_statements.exceptions: Glottalized resonants do not make a syllable heavy (exx. 21-23: stress passes over Vʔ-resonant syllables); suffix classes (hardening '!' / softening '=') change the stem-final segment's class and hence stress (gǝl- + -tud -> first-syllable stress vs gǝl- + hardening suffix -> later stress; obstruent -> resonant under a softening suffix attracts stress); plural forms with inserted glottal stop after a high vowel lose first-syllable stress (49-50); high vowels i u 'function as long vowels' (fn. 1); fn. 3 discusses an alternative formal statement (Siegel) and why a mirror-image rule would wrongly predict initial default stress; fn. 4: stem extensions and long words need further work.
new_statements.identity_note: Littell 2016 describes the Kwak’wala dialect proper (the dialect of the Kwakiutl/Kwaguł of the Fort Rupert - Alert Bay area: 'the Kwak’wala dialect itself is the specific dialect portrayed here', p. 30), naming Gwat’sala, ’Nak’wala, Gut’sala and Liq’wala as other dialects not covered; data from modern speakers, FirstVoices (2009)/Grubb (1977), Boas-Hunt texts and U’mista materials. Bach 1975 (unread) treats 'Kwakiutl' = Kwak’wala; variety not verifiable without the text.

new_statements.quote: [p. 421, A.4.1] Kwak’wala stress falls on the leftmost heavy syllable, so long as a heavy syllable exists; otherwise it falls on the rightmost syllable (Bach, 1975; Wilson, 1986; Struijke, 2000). Given the underlying forms and syllabification procedure proposed in this appendix, “heavy” just means having a +R nucleus. [p. 423, A.4.2] Words without any heavy syllables are not particularly common, but such words receive final stress: nəqʷə́ɬ 'salal berry', yəǧə́kʷ 'something knitted', xʷəp̓ə́s 'hole in the ground'. [p. 412] For the purposes of syllabification and stress, m, n, l, y, and w can pattern like vowels, the first three realized as [əm], [ən], and [əl] and the latter two surfacing as [i] and [u] respectively

new_statements.rule_in_words: Unbounded, quantity-sensitive 'default-to-opposite' stress: primary stress goes on the leftmost heavy syllable of the word, where heavy = a syllable whose nucleus is a +R segment (a full vowel, or a plain resonant m n l y w acting as nucleus, i.e. surface schwa+plain sonorant, or [i]/[u] from y/w); if the word contains no heavy syllable (only schwa nuclei with obstruent or glottalized codas), stress falls on the final syllable. Glottalized resonants and other -R segments do not make a syllable heavy; +R material syllabified as an onset is not stressable; mutation (lenition) can turn -R into +R segments which then carry stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated: sec. A.4 states only the primary-stress rule; no statement on secondary stress or footing was found in the appendix.
new_statements.exceptions: A.4.3 'Apparent violations': words with initial Ciʔ/Cuʔ (guʔdán 'horse', kuʔdzác̓i 'potato patch', giʔx̌á 'to put down', ʔul̕ígən 'wolf') take non-initial stress and are analysed as containing glottalized y̓/w̓ (not +R, so light); əʔ transcribed as aʔ gives spurious violations (wədəʔstá 'cold water', ʔəy̓əʔsú 'hand'); k̓əyós [k̓iyós] 'none' has no underlying first vowel; exclamations may take final stress regardless of structure (ʔalhaʔə́n 'silly' vs dictionary initial stress); some loanwords treat schwa as a stressable nucleus (bə́sc̓ola 'to take the bus', not bəsc̓óla); end of A.3: stress of a reduplicated form is not always predictable from its base; Grubb 1977 and the FirstVoices word list sometimes mis-assign stress in transcription (pp. 425-426, fn.).
new_statements.identity_note: Littell 2016 describes the Kwak’wala dialect proper (the dialect of the Kwakiutl/Kwaguł of the Fort Rupert - Alert Bay area: 'the Kwak’wala dialect itself is the specific dialect portrayed here', p. 30), naming Gwat’sala, ’Nak’wala, Gut’sala and Liq’wala as other dialects not covered; data from modern speakers, FirstVoices (2009)/Grubb (1977), Boas-Hunt texts and U’mista materials. Bach 1975 (unread) treats 'Kwakiutl' = Kwak’wala; variety not verifiable without the text.

readall_conflicts: The three substantive sources agree on the placement: primary stress on the leftmost heavy syllable, otherwise the final syllable ('default-to-right'). They differ on (a) what counts as heavy — Zec/Bach as reported by Noguchi and Gordon use long vowels (CVV) and CVR, while Noguchi 2011 and Siemens 2016 (with Shaw 2009) say vowel length is not contrastive and define heavy as a full (non-schwa) vowel or schwa + plain resonant coda, with Vʔ and əR' light; (b) the default case — Gordon 2000 argues Boas's data show second-syllable (non-final) stress in CV/CVO-initial stems and that final stress is attested only for CəCəCə stems in terminal position, so he finds the default-to-opposite classification inconclusive, whereas Siemens (citing Shaw 2009) and Noguchi reaffirm final stress in all-light words; (c) footing/secondary stress — descriptions are inconsistent (Boas, Grubb), iambic (Zec, Kirchner, Struijke) vs. trochaic (Kalmar, S. Wilson, Noguchi's reduplication data), unresolved. Hall 1889 is silent; Bach 1975 and Littell 2016 could not be opened.

[p. 412] For the purposes of syllabification and stress, m, n, l, y, and w can pattern like vowels, the first three realized as [əm], [ən], and [əl] and the latter two surfacing as [i] and [u] respectively

sources.quote: As noted above, the stress pattern of Kʷak̓ʷala is described in the literature as default-to-right (Wilson 1978, Wilson 1986, Shaw 2009). [...] Guc̓a follows this pattern of lexical stress. [...] Any syllable with a full vowel nucleus, or with a schwa followed by a plain resonant in coda position, will attract stress, and the first such syllable from the left edge of a word will bear primary stress. If there are only light syllables in a word, the rightmost syllable is stressed. Light syllables are those with a schwa nucleus, such as open syllables with schwa, or schwa followed by a coda obstruent (ə, əO).

sources.quote: In sum, Kwak’wala stress system can be restated as follows. Stress falls on the leftmost moraic syllable or the rightmost syllable if there is no moraic syllable in the word. ‘Moraic syllable’ refers to a syllable with a non-schwa nucleus or a plain sonorant coda. In the latter case, the nucleus is usually a non-moraic schwa. (p. 325) [On Zec 1988/1995, p. 323:] According to her analysis, primary stress falls on the leftmost syllable containing a long vowel or the rightmost syllable if there is no syllable containing a long vowel in the word. Despite its popularity, it has been pointed out that Zec’s analysis crucially relies on the controversial assumption that vowel length is contrastive in Kwak’wala (Bach et al. 2005).

sources.quote: Kwakw’ala (Boas 1947; Bach 1975; Wilson 1986) is typically described as a language with a default-to-right stress system, in which the leftmost heavy syllable (=CVV, CVR [R=sonorant]) attracts stress, otherwise the final syllable, as in (2). (p. 101) [...] Boas reports that stems with initial CV, CVO have accent on second or a later syllable (Boas, pg. 218). This leaves open the possibility that words with more than two syllables may have stress on the second syllable, which would be non-final. Such a stress pattern, which actually occurs frequently in Boas’ data, contradicts the default-to-opposite pattern. [...] Without this information, it is difficult to speak confidently of Kwakw’ala as a language with default-to-opposite stress. (p. 109)
sources.locator: p. 101 (intro, ex. 2); p. 102 (typology list); sec. 2.3.2 'Kwakw'ala' p. 109
sources.note: Argues default-to-opposite systems (Kwak'wala is a textbook case) may be reanalysable as intonational/phrasal prominence -- the basis of Elfner 2024's phrasal reanalysis; bears on the record's domain=word and any caution note, not on the placement rule.
